content:
Looks pretty interesting. ChatGPT's latest update adds Mac integration: users can handle conversations directly within the Apple Messages app. This feature supports iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

The Mac version of ChatGPT now has an Apple Messages extension.

The new Apple Messages extension allows ChatGPT to read and search your chat history on Mac, as well as compose and send messages. OpenAI says this feature is available across all ChatGPT macOS desktop app plans, and supports both ChatGPT and Codex.

Given the broad scope of permissions involved, this feature has naturally raised concerns about privacy and control. OpenAI emphasises that sending messages requires user approval by default. Users should think carefully before granting permanent approval. OpenAI's extension guidelines detail the related risks, how to revoke permissions, and a known issue involving bypassing the approval prompt.

At this stage, this feature is only available on Macs with Apple Silicon; Intel models are not supported.

If you ask ChatGPT to send a message on your behalf, the system will pop up a confirmation prompt before sending. You can also choose to skip this confirmation step in individual conversations.

Want to find this new feature in ChatGPT? The link below will take you directly to the ChatGPT for Mac Messages extension page.

Collaborative site editing, conversation snapshot sharing, and more

Although the Messages extension is the headlining new feature for Apple users this time, this update also includes a number of other improvements. For example, pinned conversations can now sync between the ChatGPT desktop app and iOS, letting users access important conversations on both Mac and iPhone whenever they want.

ChatGPT now also lets users share read-only local Codex conversation snapshots. Even if the original conversation is updated later, these snapshots will not change.

Links generated from personal accounts can be opened by anyone with the URL; however, workspace links can only be opened by members of that workspace. OpenAI says Codex will mask known sensitive formats, but reminds users to check their own snapshots, as they may still contain sensitive information.

In addition, site owners can invite existing members from the same workspace to co-edit sites with collaboration enabled. Once the owner completes the initial publish, editors can update content and database data, save versions, and publish updates. The owner retains control over access permissions, settings, analytics, and version rollback.

Some site owners can also change URLs hosted by ChatGPT without redeploying; the old address will automatically redirect to the new one.

Finally, the computer use history feature launched last week is now being expanded to Pro, Business, and Enterprise users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK. This opt-in feature requires the memory feature to be enabled first in order to work, and is off by default.

You can see the full release announcement for this update here.
